documents.abstract: Text-to-video retrieval answers user queries through searches based on concepts and embeddings. However, due to limitations in the size of the concept bank and the amount of training data, answering queries in the wild is not always effective because of the out-of-vocabulary problem. Furthermore, neither concept-based nor embedding-based search can perform reasoning to consolidate search results for complex queries that include logical and spatial constraints. To address these challenges, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to paraphrase queries using text-to-text (T2T), text-to-image (T2I), and image-to-text (I2T) transformations. These transformations rephrase abstract concepts into simpler terms to mitigate the out-of-vocabulary problem. Additionally, complex relationships within a query can be decomposed into simpler sub-queries, improving retrieval performance by effectively fusing the search results of these sub-queries. To mitigate the issue of LLM hallucination, this paper also proposes a novel consistency-based verification strategy to filter out factually incorrect paraphrased queries. Extensive experiments are conducted for ad-hoc video search and known-item search on the TRECVid datasets. We provide empirical insights into how traditionally difficult-to-answer queries can be effectively resolved through query paraphrasing.

Introduction: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) has a steep learning curve, which limits widespread adoption. Objective metrics to define surgical proficiency, efficiency, and perceived workload remain underexplored outside academic institutions. This study aimed to characterize the learning curve of HoLEP from one single surgeon at an ambulatory surgical center. Methods: A total of 103 patients underwent HoLEP for BPH between March 2024 and August 2025. Surgical cases were stratified into 3 sequential groups of 34, 34, and 35 cases, respectively, based on operative chronology. Operative characteristics were compared across groups: enucleation time, laser energy, fluid use, and enucleation speed (enucleation time/specimen weight). Perceived workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) to evaluate perceived workload across several “performance” domains (mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, and frustration). Comparisons of outcome metrics were made for 90-day postoperative complications. Urinary continence outcomes were evaluated at 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months postoperatively. Univariable and multivariable multinomial logistic regression analyses were performed to examine associations between surgical characteristics and group classification. Results: Progressive improvement was observed in operative time, enucleation time, laser energy, total fluid, enucleation speed, and NASA TLX, as seen in Table 1 . No statistically significant associations were observed between group classification and 90-day postoperative complications or urinary continence outcomes at any follow-up interval. In multivariable multinomial logistic regression analysis, the NASA-TLX score (OR 0.83, 95% CI, 0.70–0.98, p = 0.02) remained an independent predictor of higher learning curve classification. documents.abstract: Accurate evaluation of LLM personalization is hindered by current evaluation paradigms that over- or under-constrain the response space, yielding frequent false rejections and false acceptances. To reduce these false rates, we introduce ConQual-Audit, an audit-based framework that evaluates LLM personalization through a three-stage process: (1) extracting semantic constraints from user profiles and task-grounded reference; (2) qualifying constraints by pruning unnecessary constraints and recovering missing constraints; and (3) verifying candidate responses against the audited constraints via natural language inference. Across PrefEval and LaMP, ConQual-Audit outperforms nine baselines, attaining top AUCs (0.88 and 0.90) and the lowest false rate (0.21) on the leanest constraint sets at an amortizable audit cost. Crucially, this constraint audit is portable: integrating it into ExPerT and PREF helps revise smaller, higher-quality constraint sets to reduce their evaluation false rates.

This conceptual article examines how Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NMR) framework can provide orientation during periods of social disruption. It translates six fundamental human needs—thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realization and participation, and meaning—into five practical mindsets: identifying needs behind conflicts; gaining control through understanding and participation; considering everyone affected; working through competing requirements; and sharing knowledge to develop solutions. The article’s specific contribution is an explicit connection between basic needs, cognitive orientations, decision practices and institutional consequences. A hypothetical public-service conflict illustrates how these mindsets can inform diagnosis, deliberation, decision-making and follow-up. An evaluation agenda distinguishes improvements in understanding, judgment, participation and material living conditions. Within the developing NMR and human–AI corpus, the paper adds an application layer focused on crisis orientation and collective agency. It connects the framework’s anthropological and normative foundations with practical questions of democratic governance and Learning by Teaching (LdL). The article presents a conceptual operationalization and proposals for empirical assessment. Prepared through dialogue between Jean-Pol Martin and ChatGPT.

Sycophancy, where an LLM becomes overly agreeable, deferential, or flattering toward the user, has been identified as a major failure mode. While post-training has been implicated as a cause, how it internally gives rise to sycophantic behavior remains insufficiently understood. Post-training transforms the model's output from text completion into utterances directed toward an addressee, thereby giving the output \textit{addressivity}. We hypothesize that the accompanying pressure to follow the addressee's instructions and align with their preferences links this addressivity to sycophancy. To test this, we use Sparse Autoencoders to extract addressivity directions from pre-trained and post-trained models and examine their relationship with sycophancy. Steering models with addressivity directions can amplify or suppress sycophancy, and this effect is observed only in post-trained models. Furthermore, comparing the internal mechanisms of both model types confirms that the association between addressivity and sycophancy is strengthened through post-training. Finally, through a controlled post-training experiment, we find that models are sycophantic not toward a specific addressee but toward any recognized addressee, suggesting that the presence of an addressee, rather than the addressee's identity, is what elicits sycophancy.

documents.abstract: Abstract For the health sector, novel applications involving automated decision-making (ADM) and artificial intelligence (AI) are seen as a way to fill critical gaps in health systems and improve patient care and outcomes. For patients, carers, and health consumers more broadly, these innovations may be viewed as a way to improve their agency and understanding of their bodies and health states. Yet, many of the devices and software remain speculative or in limited pilot testing. In this chapter, we discuss findings from a project that sought to identify the socio-technical imaginaries of ADM and AI in health in Australia, comparing “actually existing ADM” with proposed imaginaries of the futures of ADM. We mapped how emerging health technologies are discussed in industry reports and websites. Our findings reveal that these complex assemblages of people, objects, data, spaces, systems, promises, expectations, and proximities generate a number of ethical issues and power dynamics.

documents.abstract: This article aimed to analyze the changes in reference services resulting from the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and generative AI, identifying ethical, conceptual, and operational challenges, as well as the new skills and educational guidelines required for information professionals. It used a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive bibliographic and documentary research method, based on contemporary literature on Information Science, information mediation, and emerging technologies in education. It highlights that automation and conversational assistants (like chatbots and recommendation systems) streamline operational processes and speed up access and personalization of searches; however, human mediation remains essential to ensure information literacy, critical evaluation of sources, accuracy in data retrieval, and mitigation of algorithmic hallucinations. It can be concluded that artificial intelligence doesn’t replace the librarian, but rather reshapes their role for strategic tasks, ethical oversight, and digital curation, showing that the future of reference services lies in the convergence of technological efficiency and humanized mediation.

Military occupational health and safety (OHS) is inseparable from operational readiness, personnel welfare and the long-term sustainability of armed forces. Nigerian Air Force personnel, infantry soldiers and mechanized armoured-vehicle crews encounter overlapping but occupationally distinctive hazards: aircraft noise and vibration, jet-fuel and exhaust exposure, fatigue and high-consequence decision-making in aviation; combat trauma, heavy load carriage, heat strain, sleep disruption and musculoskeletal injury among infantry; and whole-body vibration, acoustic trauma, restricted egress, heat, fumes and communication difficulties among armoured crews. This article examines these risks in Nigeria while drawing comparisons with research and prevention approaches from Europe, North America and other military settings. It adopts a structured narrative literature review methodology, synthesising peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, occupational health guidance, and relevant Nigerian studies published mainly between 2023 and 2026, alongside foundational work where recent evidence is limited. Recent reviews show that military and law-enforcement populations experience a broad spectrum of adverse outcomes, including mental ill-health, hearing loss, musculoskeletal disorders, heat illness, sleep problems and burnout. Nigerian evidence identifies psychological distress among deployed soldiers and air-force personnel, while international studies provide more detailed evidence on load carriage, jet-fuel exposure, fatigue, noise and vibration. The article argues that Nigeria requires a role-specific, prevention-led military OHS system supported by exposure monitoring, confidential health surveillance, fatigue-risk management, equipment maintenance, heat controls, hearing conservation, post-deployment support and a stronger local research programme. Because available Nigerian studies are often cross-sectional or facility-specific, international findings should inform, not substitute for local exposure measurement and longitudinal research.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This study evaluates the intersection of socio-economic vulnerabilities and occupational health hazards among tribal women in India. Drawing exclusively upon secondary data, government reports and academic literature, the paper highlights that an overwhelming majority of tribal women are concentrated in primary sectors-predominantly agriculture, minor forest produce collection and unorganized manual labor. Despite serving as the backbone of the tribal agrarian and forest-based economy, they face severe structural disadvantages, including deep-seated illiteracy, acute poverty, geographic isolation and an absence of ergonomically sound tools. Consequently, they experience disproportionate rates of musculoskeletal disorders, chronic fatigue, dermatological infections, vector-borne diseases and respiratory complications. The findings indicate that poor socio-economic status directly exacerbates occupational vulnerability, compounded by an acute lack of institutional healthcare infrastructure in remote tribal habitations.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) has become an increasingly important concern in India as industrialisation, urbanisation, technological development, and the expansion of employment continue to reshape the world of work. Workplace safety is no longer limited to preventing machinery-related accidents or physical injuries. Workers may face chemical exposure, biological risks, unsafe equipment, poor ergonomics, occupational diseases, excessive working hours, workplace violence, stress, and other psychosocial risks. These concerns exist across sectors, including construction, manufacturing, mining, chemical industries, agriculture, informal employment, and healthcare. India has developed a substantial legal framework for protecting workers, culminating in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which came into force on November 21, 2025. However, the existence of legislation alone cannot guarantee safe working conditions. The continuing occurrence of workplace accidents, under-reporting of occupational diseases, inadequate safety infrastructure, and institutional failures demonstrate the need for stronger implementation and accountability. Recent attention to workplace safety following the R.G. Kar Medical College incident has further shown that occupational safety also includes dignity, security, gender-sensitive protection, and psychological well-being. The central concern, therefore, should be to move from a culture that reacts to accidents towards one that identifies and prevents risks before workers are harmed. Keywords: Occupational Safety and Health; Occupational Hazards; Workplace Safety; Occupational Diseases; Worker Protection.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This working paper sets out the theoretical foundations of the Operational Continuity and Turnaround Architecture (OCTA), a domain-free quantitative model for predicting, detecting and arresting operational collapse in complex sociotechnical systems. The two core constructs are the Dependency Cascade Index (DCI), which measures the ratio of active dependencies to remaining recovery capacity in real time, and the intervention window W(t), which measures the time remaining before DCI crosses the irreversible collapse threshold. Together these constructs enable early detection of cascade propagation and provide a formal basis for turnaround intervention before collapse becomes irreversible. The model is validated primarily in civil aviation, using GNSS interference and ADS-B signal degradation as observable proxies for DCI dynamics. Domain-independence of the W(t) mechanism is demonstrated across banking and financial systems, automotive supply chains, nuclear energy, maritime operations, power grid infrastructure and healthcare systems. This working paper is part of a PhD research programme at Cranfield University. The commercial implementation of OCTA is developed through the TYRAXE technology stack (AIX, LINK, FLOW). Patent pending.

Recent work in tabular machine learning has emphasized the importance of diverse and realistic evaluation settings. The niche of large-scale (1M+) data, however, remains under-explored. To study training-data scaling, we assemble eight real-world tabular datasets with up to around ten million training examples, retaining the natural distribution shifts of the tasks and using random-split evaluation as a control. We find that GBDTs and MLP-based models show broadly similar scaling trends, with gains from both additional training data and algorithmic improvements. Tabular foundation models show more varied scaling behavior, with recent versions benefiting more consistently from larger contexts even under distribution shift. However, scaling training data under distribution shift introduces new challenges: in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance mostly improve together at smaller scales but can diverge at larger scales. We examine this through MLP capacity sweeps and comparisons of the validation distributions used for tuning and early stopping in MLPs and GBDTs. We also compare common practices of using validation data, contrasting its use for model selection in MLP pipelines with using it for in-context fitting in tabular foundation model pipelines. Under stronger shifts, MLPs selected using validation representative of the evaluation conditions generally maintain or improve performance as training data grows. In contrast, including such examples in context improves foundation-model performance, but does not prevent deterioration with increasing training size in our experiments.

Multi-agent LLM systems can formalize natural-language argumentation end-to-end, turning plain text into structured graphs by classifying components, connecting them with relations, and enriching the resulting graphs into formal models. Quality assurance for those graphs is almost always another LLMs: a reviewer, judge, or critic agent. On the other side, in adjacent neuro-symbolic fields, such generated output is often verified symbolically by external checks and solvers. In this work, we argue that in argument graph verification, the allocation should be similar, and based on what each instrument can guarantee. We propose layered verification: starting from deterministic checks, moving to solver-based and LLM reviews, and utilizing debate only under uncertainty, leaving human judgment for what no other instrument can decide. We ground our principle with a study on human-annotated graphs with injected structural defects. An LLM reviewer detects them at near-ceiling recall, including cycles in the support relation, but it objects to almost one in a ten correct graphs, even though it should not, happens to be inconsistent in verdict on identical inputs and is significantly slower than the equivalent exact check. It shows that while LLM reviewer does not lack the ability to detect structural defects, it is worth having a deterministic verification gates.

ORBITAL ARCHAEOLOGY: THE AI EARTH MAPPER TV Series Format Bible & Pitch Deck LOGLINE: Over 90% of human history remains buried beneath dense canopy, desert sands, and coastline sediments. By fusing multispectral satellite imaging, predictive AI algorithms, and precision drone LiDAR, an elite investigative team reveals lost cities and forgotten empires in real time — straight from orbit to the ground. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: Traditional archaeology is slow, costly, and bound by bureaucratic restrictions. "Orbital Archaeology: The AI Earth Mapper" revolutionizes the genre by taking exploration into the 21st century. Rather than digging blindly, the series utilizes satellite multispectral signatures (infrared, thermal, and moisture retention analysis) processed by custom Artificial Intelligence. The AI pinpoints subterranean structural anomalies invisible to the human eye. Once targets are identified, an agile field team deploys heavy-duty drones equipped with LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) to "erase" surface vegetation on screen, revealing 3D structural models of buried ruins before ground-penetrating radar confirms the discovery. BACKGROUND: The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs). OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations. DESIGN: Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective. SETTING: Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026. PARTICIPANTS: No human participants were involved. MEASUREMENTS: Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action). RESULTS: The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%). LIMITATIONS: Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use. CONCLUSION: The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations. PRIMARY FUNDING SOURCE: None.

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Surgical palliative care (SPC) research has advanced since the 2017 research agenda, but persistent gaps in patient selection, intervention delivery, and outcome measurement limit implementation across evolving surgical care settings. STUDY DESIGN: In November 2025, a national consensus conference convened 28 SPC experts and researchers. Through iterative discussion and consensus-building during the meeting and subsequent months, participants updated research priorities across the surgical continuum and health system context. Full methodology and participant attributes were described in Supplemental Materials https://links.lww.com/JACS/A821. RESULTS: The updated agenda identified 11 research gaps across 3 priority areas: patient selection; interventions, care processes, and competencies; and outcome measurement. Priorities were mapped at 2 levels: surgical episodes, encompassing patient-, family-, and provider-level factors, and health systems, encompassing organizational and structural factors affecting SPC delivery. The agenda prioritizes identifying which patients benefit from SPC and when; broadening SPC beyond traditional populations; defining primary SPC competencies and the role of specialty consultation; improving communication of surgical intent, trade-offs, and preference-sensitive decisions; integrating and sustaining SPC across heterogeneous systems and care transitions; transforming clinical cultures; and developing patient-centered, context-specific surgical and systems-level outcomes. Emerging electronic health record, natural language processing, and large language model approaches may support scalable patient identification, intervention delivery, and outcome measurement, while requiring attention to bias and task-dependent performance. CONCLUSIONS: SPC research should move beyond narrow proof-of-concept settings toward pragmatic, scalable approaches that define who should receive SPC, what should be delivered, and how success should be measured across diverse surgical environments.

This study investigates how a structured “paper-first” approach can support cognitive engagement during artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted academic work in higher education. Growing reliance on generative AI has increased concerns about surface-level learning, trial-and-error prompting, and reduced student ownership of academic writing. Using a two-year design-based research approach involving nine iterative cycles, the study developed and refined a framework that required students to construct manual logic diagrams before engaging with AI tools and expert system environments. Participants included a six-member interdisciplinary design team and 150 communication for academic purposes students from the faculty of information and communications technology at a South African university. Data were collected through iterative observations and focus group interviews and analyzed using grounded theory and constant comparative analysis. Findings indicate that the framework supported more structured reasoning, reduced inefficient prompting behaviors, and improved students’ ability to identify weaknesses in their own arguments before digital interaction. Students also reported increased confidence and greater ownership of their academic work. The study argues that structured pre-AI planning activities can strengthen critical thinking and academic literacy by positioning AI as a support tool rather than a substitute for cognitive effort. The findings contribute practical guidance for educators seeking to integrate AI into higher education while preserving student agency and deep learning.
